entities.name: Carmine Caracciolo, 5th Prince of Santo Buono
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Carmine Nicolao Caracciolo, 5th Prince of Santo Buono, Grandee of Spain, served as the Spanish Viceroy of Peru from October 5, 1716, to January 26, 1720. A Neapolitan nobleman appointed by King Philip V, the first Bourbon monarch of Spain, Caracciolo's viceroyalty marked a pivotal moment in the implementation of the Bourbon Reforms in Spanish South America. His administration was tasked with reasserting royal authority, increasing revenue extraction, and improving colonial defense following the War of the Spanish Succession, which had severely weakened the Spanish Crown's grip on its overseas territories. Caracciolo's tenure aimed to rationalize the complex administrative and economic structures of Peru, a key node in the global Spanish Empire.

During his relatively brief term, Caracciolo focused on several critical areas. Economically, he worked to combat contraband trade, particularly with British and Dutch merchants, by enforcing stricter customs controls and attempting to revive the traditional fleet system. He also grappled with the chronic issues of the mita system and the exploitation of indigenous labor, though without revolutionary changes. Militarily, he strengthened coastal defenses against piracy and foreign incursions, a persistent threat to the lucrative silver routes from Potosí. Perhaps his most enduring challenge was navigating the complex relationship between secular colonial power and the entrenched influence of the Church, particularly concerning ecclesiastical privileges and the vast wealth accumulated by religious orders in Peru. His administration also oversaw the initial recovery efforts following the devastating 1716 Lima earthquake.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Carmine Caracciolo's viceroyalty in Peru (1716-1720) was a crucial early phase in the implementation of the Bourbon Reforms in South America, directly influencing the administrative and economic restructuring of one of Spain's wealthiest colonies. His efforts to combat contraband and centralize power laid groundwork for subsequent, more radical changes.
